expectedText:
SOCIAL PURPOSE CORPORATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Social Purpose Corporation

SOCIAL PURPOSE CORPORATION — WHAT THIS INFORMATION SHEET COVERS
This information sheet describes California's Social Purpose Corporations Act, Corporations Code Division 1.5 (§§ 2500-3503) — a distinct for-profit corporate form under California's General Corporation Law, separate from an ordinary for-profit corporation and separate from this corpus's existing Benefit Corporation information sheet, which covers a different statute (Corp. Code Part 13, §§ 14600-14631) with its own purpose language, its own annual-report content, and its own enforcement mechanism. A social purpose corporation is formed by filing articles of incorporation with the California Secretary of State that state both a general business purpose and one or more enumerated "special purposes," and it is subject to recurring reporting obligations tied to those special purposes that a regular corporation does not have. Acme Social Purpose Corporation is considering, or has adopted, this form for its California operations.

This sheet states facts about the statute: what the articles must and may contain, how a director's statutory duty of care is defined for this specific corporate form, what the statute says about who a social purpose corporation's assets and purposes actually run to, and what recurring shareholder reports the statute requires and when. It does NOT draft a full set of articles of incorporation, bylaws, or an annual report; it does not tell Acme Social Purpose Corporation whether the social purpose corporation form, the benefit corporation form, or an ordinary corporation is the right choice for its specific business or fundraising plans; it does not evaluate any specific special-purpose language for legal sufficiency; and it does not address the separate question of what happens to a pre-2015 "flexible purpose corporation" that has not amended its articles, beyond stating what the statute itself says about that scenario.

THE SOCIAL PURPOSE CORPORATIONS ACT AND ITS 2011 PREDECESSOR
California's statute governing this entity form states its own name: "This division shall be known and may be cited as the Social Purpose Corporations Act." That name is not the one the Legislature originally used. The division was enacted in 2011 (Stats. 2011, Ch. 740) creating the "flexible purpose corporation," and the Legislature later renamed the form via SB 1301 (Stats. 2014, Ch. 694), effective January 1, 2015, substituting "social purpose corporation" throughout. The statute did not force existing entities to convert. A pre-2015 flexible purpose corporation may elect the new name by amending its articles — the statute states a corporation "may elect to change its status from a flexible purpose corporation to a social purpose corporation by amending its articles of incorporation to change its name to replace “flexible purpose corporation” with “social purpose corporation” and to replace the term “flexible purpose corporation” with “social purpose corporation” as applicable in any statements contained in the articles." — but a corporation that has not made that amendment keeps operating under the old name and the old statutory label: "For any flexible purpose corporation formed before January 1, 2015, that has not amended its articles of incorporation to change its status to a social purpose corporation, any reference in this division to social purpose corporation shall be deemed a reference to “flexible purpose corporation.”" The division's scope provision confirms the same continuity from the other direction, stating that the division applies to social purpose corporations "including all flexible purpose corporations formed under this division prior to January 1, 2015, and now existing"

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This division shall be known and may be cited as the Social Purpose Corporations Act."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2500, Social Purpose Corporations Act, statutory short title (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2500.)
  "may elect to change its status from a flexible purpose corporation to a social purpose corporation by amending its articles of incorporation to change its name to replace “flexible purpose corporation” with “social purpose corporation” and to replace the term “flexible purpose corporation” with “social purpose corporation” as applicable in any statements contained in the articles."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2601(b)(3), Social Purpose Corporations Act, election to rename a flexible purpose corporation and the default rule for one that has not elected (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2601.)
  "For any flexible purpose corporation formed before January 1, 2015, that has not amended its articles of incorporation to change its status to a social purpose corporation, any reference in this division to social purpose corporation shall be deemed a reference to “flexible purpose corporation.”"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2601(b)(3), Social Purpose Corporations Act, deemed reference to "flexible purpose corporation" absent an amendment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2601.)
  "including all flexible purpose corporations formed under this division prior to January 1, 2015, and now existing"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2502, Social Purpose Corporations Act, scope provision covering pre-2015 flexible purpose corporations still existing under that name (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2502.)
  Known gap: This is the current text of a division that has been amended repeatedly since 2011 (most recently by 2022 and 2023 chaptering shown in the fetched sections' own history notes); it does not track every intermediate version of the statute, only the version in force as of the checked date. It also does not identify whether any specific existing entity is, in fact, an unconverted flexible purpose corporation — that is a question about that entity's own articles of incorporation, not about the statute.

THE GENERAL CORPORATION LAW FILLS IN EVERYTHING THE ACT DOES NOT SAY
A social purpose corporation is not governed only by Division 1.5. The statute makes California's general, Division 1 corporate law the default backdrop: "Except as otherwise expressly stated, the provisions of Division 1 (commencing with Section 100) shall apply to corporations organized under this division" In practice this means that matters this division does not address for a social purpose corporation — such as most shareholder meeting, voting, and inspection mechanics — are governed by the same General Corporation Law provisions that apply to an ordinary for-profit corporation, unless Division 1.5 itself states a different rule for social purpose corporations specifically.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as otherwise expressly stated, the provisions of Division 1 (commencing with Section 100) shall apply to corporations organized under this division"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2501, Social Purpose Corporations Act, incorporation by reference of the General Corporation Law (Division 1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2501.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general incorporation-by-reference rule only; it does not catalog every Division 1 section that applies, and it does not resolve a conflict between a specific Division 1.5 provision and a specific Division 1 provision for facts not addressed here — that requires reading both provisions together for the particular question at hand.

FORMATION BY FILING ARTICLES, AND THE REQUIRED NAME ELEMENT
A social purpose corporation is formed the same basic way as any other California corporation — by filing articles with the Secretary of State. The statute states: "One or more natural persons, partnerships, associations, social purpose corporations, or corporations, domestic or foreign, may form a social purpose corporation under this division by executing and filing articles of incorporation." and that "The corporate existence begins upon the filing of the articles and continues perpetually, unless otherwise expressly provided by law or in the articles." The articles must also flag the entity's form in its own name: the statute requires "The name of the social purpose corporation that shall contain the words “social purpose corporation” or an abbreviation of those words."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "One or more natural persons, partnerships, associations, social purpose corporations, or corporations, domestic or foreign, may form a social purpose corporation under this division by executing and filing articles of incorporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2600(a), Social Purpose Corporations Act, formation by filing articles of incorporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2600.)
  "The corporate existence begins upon the filing of the articles and continues perpetually, unless otherwise expressly provided by law or in the articles."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2600(c), Social Purpose Corporations Act, corporate existence begins on filing and continues perpetually absent a contrary provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2600.)
  "The name of the social purpose corporation that shall contain the words “social purpose corporation” or an abbreviation of those words."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2602(a), Social Purpose Corporations Act, required name element (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2602.)
  Known gap: This clause covers only the act-of-filing and naming mechanics stated in this division; it does not restate the Secretary of State's separate name-distinguishability rules that apply to corporations generally under Division 1, and it does not address the filing fee, which the statute (Corp. Code § 2502.05) sets by cross-reference to the Government Code fee schedule for corporations generally rather than stating a dollar figure itself.

THE ARTICLES MUST STATE BOTH A GENERAL PURPOSE AND AN ENUMERATED SPECIAL PURPOSE
What sets this entity form apart from an ordinary corporation is not the filing mechanics — it is what the articles must say about purpose. The statute requires a general-purpose statement drawn from a prescribed form; a corporation not organized to practice a licensed profession must state that "The purpose of this social purpose corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a social purpose corporation may be organized under Division 1.5 of the California Corporations Code" (with the corporation's own enumerated purposes filled in). Beyond that general statement, the articles must separately include "A statement that a purpose of the social purpose corporation, in addition to the purpose stated pursuant to paragraph (1), is to engage in one or more of the following enumerated purposes" one of the following two statutory categories: first, "One or more charitable or public purpose activities that a nonprofit public benefit corporation is authorized to carry out." or second, "The purpose of promoting positive effects of, or minimizing adverse effects of, the social purpose corporation’s activities upon any of the following, provided that the corporation consider the purpose in addition to or together with the financial interests of the shareholders and compliance with legal obligations, and take action consistent with that purpose:" — followed by a list of specific beneficiaries the statute itself supplies: the corporation's employees, suppliers, customers, and creditors; the community and society; or the environment. "Special purpose," as a defined statutory term, means exactly this articles-stated purpose: "“Special purpose” means the special purpose set forth in a social purpose corporation’s articles pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 2602."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The purpose of this social purpose corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a social purpose corporation may be organized under Division 1.5 of the California Corporations Code"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2602(b)(1)(A), Social Purpose Corporations Act, required general purpose statement for a non-professional social purpose corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2602.)
  "A statement that a purpose of the social purpose corporation, in addition to the purpose stated pursuant to paragraph (1), is to engage in one or more of the following enumerated purposes"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2602(b)(2), Social Purpose Corporations Act, required additional special-purpose statement and its lead-in language (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2602.)
  "One or more charitable or public purpose activities that a nonprofit public benefit corporation is authorized to carry out."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2602(b)(2)(A), Social Purpose Corporations Act, first enumerated special-purpose category (public-benefit-type activities) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2602.)
  "The purpose of promoting positive effects of, or minimizing adverse effects of, the social purpose corporation’s activities upon any of the following, provided that the corporation consider the purpose in addition to or together with the financial interests of the shareholders and compliance with legal obligations, and take action consistent with that purpose:"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2602(b)(2)(B), Social Purpose Corporations Act, second enumerated special-purpose category (stakeholder and environmental effects) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2602.)
  "“Special purpose” means the special purpose set forth in a social purpose corporation’s articles pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 2602."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2513, Social Purpose Corporations Act, statutory definition of "special purpose" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2513.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the two statutory purpose categories and their required lead-in language; it does not draft the specific enumerated purpose to insert into either blank, does not address the separate prescribed purpose statement for a professional social purpose corporation (Corp. Code § 2602(b)(1)(B)) or for one subject to the Banking Law or Insurance Code (Corp. Code § 2602(b)(4)-(5)), and does not evaluate whether any specific proposed purpose text would satisfy the statute — that is a drafting judgment about the specific language chosen, not a fact this sheet can state in the abstract.

GENERAL BUSINESS POWERS, BOUNDED BY THE CORPORATION'S OWN STATED SPECIAL PURPOSE
Once formed, a social purpose corporation has broad business powers, but the statute makes those powers expressly conditional on the purpose the corporation put in its own articles: "Subject to any limitation contained in the articles, to compliance with any other applicable laws, and to consistency with the special purpose of the social purpose corporation, any social purpose corporation other than a social purpose corporation subject to the Banking Law or a professional social purpose corporation may engage in any business activity."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Subject to any limitation contained in the articles, to compliance with any other applicable laws, and to consistency with the special purpose of the social purpose corporation, any social purpose corporation other than a social purpose corporation subject to the Banking Law or a professional social purpose corporation may engage in any business activity."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2604, Social Purpose Corporations Act, general business powers conditioned on consistency with the corporation's special purpose (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2604.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general powers rule and its express purpose-consistency condition; it does not identify what counts as an activity inconsistent with a specific corporation's stated special purpose, which depends on the actual purpose language that corporation adopted, nor does it address the separate,  narrower powers rules that apply to a social purpose corporation subject to the Banking Law or organized as a professional corporation, which the same section (Corp. Code § 2604) addresses in its second sentence.

A DIRECTOR'S STATUTORY DUTY OF CARE, INCLUDING THE CORPORATION'S STATED PURPOSES AS A FACTOR
This division sets its own director standard-of-care statute for a social purpose corporation, separate from the general corporate business-judgment-rule statute (Corp. Code § 309) that governs an ordinary corporation's directors. The core standard is worded the same way: "A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and with that care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances." But the factors a director is told to weigh are not the same. The statute states that "In discharging his or her duties, a director shall consider those factors, and give weight to those factors, as the director deems relevant, including the overall prospects of the social purpose corporation, the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and the purposes of the social purpose corporation as set forth in its articles." — expressly listing the articles-stated purposes of the social purpose corporation as one of the factors a director may consider and weigh, alongside the corporation's prospects and the shareholders' best interests, in a way the general corporate business-judgment-rule statute for an ordinary corporation does not.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and with that care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2700(a), Social Purpose Corporations Act, director's core statutory duty of care (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2700.)
  "In discharging his or her duties, a director shall consider those factors, and give weight to those factors, as the director deems relevant, including the overall prospects of the social purpose corporation, the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and the purposes of the social purpose corporation as set forth in its articles."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2700(c), Social Purpose Corporations Act, statutory factors a director may weigh, including the corporation's articles-stated purposes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2700.)
  Known gap: This clause states the statutory factors a director is permitted to consider; it does not state that a director is required to act on the special purpose in any particular instance — the statute's own wording gives the director discretion to decide how much weight each factor gets — and it does not address how a court would apply this standard to any specific board decision, since no California appellate authority construing this specific director-duty section was located in this research pass (see the CourtListener search note in this document's supporting research).

THE SPECIAL PURPOSE DOES NOT MAKE THE CORPORATION HOLD ASSETS FOR, OR OWE DUTIES TO, OUTSIDERS
Naming a stakeholder group or the environment in the articles' special-purpose statement does not give that group or the environment an enforceable stake in the corporation. The statute is direct about this: "Notwithstanding any of the purposes set forth in its articles, a social purpose corporation shall not be deemed to hold any of its assets for the benefit of any party other than its shareholders." — though the same subdivision preserves separately existing law by adding that "nothing in this division shall be construed as negating existing charitable trust principles or the Attorney General’s authority to enforce any charitable trust created." The following subdivision closes the loop for directors specifically: "Nothing in this section, express or implied, is intended to create or grant or shall create or grant any right in or for any person or any cause of action by or for any person, and a director shall not be responsible to any party other than the social purpose corporation and its shareholders."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Notwithstanding any of the purposes set forth in its articles, a social purpose corporation shall not be deemed to hold any of its assets for the benefit of any party other than its shareholders."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2700(e), Social Purpose Corporations Act, statement that the corporation does not hold assets for the benefit of any party other than its shareholders (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2700.)
  "nothing in this division shall be construed as negating existing charitable trust principles or the Attorney General’s authority to enforce any charitable trust created."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2700(e), Social Purpose Corporations Act, preservation of existing charitable trust law and Attorney General enforcement authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2700.)
  "Nothing in this section, express or implied, is intended to create or grant or shall create or grant any right in or for any person or any cause of action by or for any person, and a director shall not be responsible to any party other than the social purpose corporation and its shareholders."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2700(f), Social Purpose Corporations Act, no third-party right or cause of action created; director responsible only to the corporation and its shareholders (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2700.)
  Known gap: This clause states what the statute itself says about who may enforce a social purpose corporation's special purpose and who its assets are held for; it does not address whether a different body of law outside this division — such as a specific charitable trust already in existence, or a separate contractual promise the corporation made to a named stakeholder — could independently create an enforceable right, since the statute expressly carves out that possibility without itself resolving whether one exists in any given case.

THE ANNUAL REPORT: FINANCIAL STATEMENTS PLUS A SPECIAL PURPOSE MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS
A social purpose corporation's board has a recurring, statute-driven reporting duty to its own shareholders. The statute states a deadline: "The board of a social purpose corporation shall cause an annual report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 120 days after the close of the fiscal year." Beyond ordinary financial statements, the same section requires a distinct narrative document: "The board shall cause to be provided with the annual report, a management discussion and analysis (special purpose MD&A) concerning the social purpose corporation’s stated purpose or purposes as set forth in its articles pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 2602, and, to the extent consistent with reasonable confidentiality requirements, shall cause the special purpose MD&A to be made publicly available by posting it on the social purpose corporation’s Internet Web site or providing it through similar electronic means."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The board of a social purpose corporation shall cause an annual report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 120 days after the close of the fiscal year."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 3500(a), Social Purpose Corporations Act, 120-day deadline for the annual report to shareholders (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=3500.)
  "The board shall cause to be provided with the annual report, a management discussion and analysis (special purpose MD&A) concerning the social purpose corporation’s stated purpose or purposes as set forth in its articles pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 2602, and, to the extent consistent with reasonable confidentiality requirements, shall cause the special purpose MD&A to be made publicly available by posting it on the social purpose corporation’s Internet Web site or providing it through similar electronic means."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 3500(b), Social Purpose Corporations Act, required special purpose management discussion and analysis (special purpose MD&A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=3500.)
  Known gap: This clause covers the annual report and special purpose MD&A requirement running to shareholders under this division; it does not address the separate, narrower exception for a corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record (covered in this document's small-corporation clause) or the separate compliance path available to a corporation already reporting under the federal Securities Exchange Act (Corp. Code § 3502(h)), and it is not a claim that this reporting duty is the same as, or satisfies, the different annual benefit report this corpus's Benefit Corporation document describes for the separate benefit-corporation statute.

A SEPARATE, EVENT-TRIGGERED "SPECIAL PURPOSE CURRENT REPORT" BETWEEN ANNUAL REPORTS
Beyond the annual report, this division imposes an interim reporting duty that does not have a counterpart in this corpus's existing Benefit Corporation document. The statute requires: "The board shall cause a special purpose current report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 45 days following the occurrence of any one or more of the events specified in subdivision (b) or (c)" Among the triggering events the same section lists is a board or management decision to "Determine that the special purpose has been satisfied or should no longer be pursued, whether temporarily or permanently."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The board shall cause a special purpose current report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 45 days following the occurrence of any one or more of the events specified in subdivision (b) or (c)"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 3501(a), Social Purpose Corporations Act, 45-day deadline for a special purpose current report following a triggering event (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=3501.)
  "Determine that the special purpose has been satisfied or should no longer be pursued, whether temporarily or permanently."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 3501(c)(2), Social Purpose Corporations Act, one statutory triggering event for a special purpose current report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=3501.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the reporting deadline and one of several statutory triggering events; it does not list every triggering event the same section defines (material expenditures and withheld planned expenditures are also covered, in Corp. Code § 3501(b) and (c)(1), and are not quoted here), and it does not address the good-faith forward-looking-statement liability exclusion the statute separately provides for these reports (Corp. Code § 3502(d)).

A NARROWER FINANCIAL-STATEMENT STANDARD FOR A SOCIAL PURPOSE CORPORATION WITH FEW SHAREHOLDERS
The statute relaxes the accounting standard for the financial statements required in the annual and current reports for a small social purpose corporation: "The financial statements of any social purpose corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record of its shares, determined as provided in Section 605, required to be furnished by Sections 3500 and 3501 are not required to be prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles if they reasonably set forth the assets and liabilities and the income and expense of the social purpose corporation and disclose the accounting basis used in their preparation."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The financial statements of any social purpose corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record of its shares, determined as provided in Section 605, required to be furnished by Sections 3500 and 3501 are not required to be prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles if they reasonably set forth the assets and liabilities and the income and expense of the social purpose corporation and disclose the accounting basis used in their preparation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 3502(g), Social Purpose Corporations Act, relaxed financial-statement standard for a corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=3502.)
  Known gap: This clause states the numeric shareholder-count threshold and the alternative disclosure standard the statute substitutes for GAAP; it does not address how "holders of record," cross-referenced to Corp. Code § 605, is counted in any specific ownership structure (for example, shares held in street name or through a nominee), which depends on the facts of that structure.

PERSONAL LIABILITY FOR A FALSE ANNUAL OR CURRENT REPORT
The statute attaches personal liability to a false statutory report. It states that "Any officers, directors, employees, or agents of a social purpose corporation who do any of the following shall be liable jointly and severally for all the damages resulting therefrom to the social purpose corporation or any person injured by those actions who relied on those actions or to both:" — and one of the listed acts triggering that liability is to "Make, issue, deliver, or publish any prospectus, report, including the reports required pursuant to Sections 3500 and 3501, circular, certificate, financial statement, balance sheet, public notice, or document respecting the social purpose corporation or its shares, assets, liabilities, capital, dividends, business, earnings, or accounts which is false in any material respect, knowing it to be false, or participate in the making, issuance, delivery, or publication thereof with knowledge that the same is false in a material respect."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any officers, directors, employees, or agents of a social purpose corporation who do any of the following shall be liable jointly and severally for all the damages resulting therefrom to the social purpose corporation or any person injured by those actions who relied on those actions or to both:"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 3503, Social Purpose Corporations Act, introductory joint-and-several liability standard for a false statutory report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=3503.)
  "Make, issue, deliver, or publish any prospectus, report, including the reports required pursuant to Sections 3500 and 3501, circular, certificate, financial statement, balance sheet, public notice, or document respecting the social purpose corporation or its shares, assets, liabilities, capital, dividends, business, earnings, or accounts which is false in any material respect, knowing it to be false, or participate in the making, issuance, delivery, or publication thereof with knowledge that the same is false in a material respect."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 3503(a), Social Purpose Corporations Act, liability for knowingly publishing a false report respecting the corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=3503.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the introductory liability standard and one of the four listed acts that trigger it (Corp. Code § 3503(a)); the other three listed acts — false book or record entries, altering records with intent to deceive, and a knowing material omission from a required report — are not separately quoted here. This clause does not address how a court would apply the knowledge and materiality requirements to any specific report's contents.

SPECIAL PURPOSE AND AGENT DECLARATION
Acme Social Purpose Corporation states, for informational purposes and not as a filed articles provision, its intended special purpose under Corporations Code § 2602(b)(2) as follows: promoting positive environmental effects of the corporation's operations.

Principal office address: 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814.

Agent for service of process: Jane Doe, at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814.

Authorized shares: 10,000,000 shares of common stock.

Nothing stated in this declaration is itself the filed articles of incorporation, and this declaration does not certify that the special-purpose language above satisfies Corporations Code § 2602(b)(2).

INCORPORATOR ACKNOWLEDGMENT AND SIGNATURE
The undersigned, Jane Doe, acknowledges reviewing this information sheet concerning the California Social Purpose Corporations Act and understands that this document is informational only, does not constitute legal advice about Acme Social Purpose Corporation's specific circumstances, and does not itself form, register, or amend any corporation.

Signature: _____________________________   Date: _____________
Jane Doe, Incorporator

Code Part 13, §§ 14600-14631) with its own purpose language, its own annual-report content, and its own enforcement mechanism. A social purpose corporation is formed by filing articles of incorporation with the California Secretary of State that state both a general business purpose and one or more enumerated "special purposes," and it is subject to recurring reporting obligations tied to those special purposes that a regular corporation does not have. Acme Social Purpose Corporation is considering, or has adopted, this form for its California operations.

This sheet states facts about the statute: what the articles must and may contain, how a director's statutory duty of care is defined for this specific corporate form, what the statute says about who a social purpose corporation's assets and purposes actually run to, and what recurring shareholder reports the statute requires and when. It does NOT draft a full set of articles of incorporation, bylaws, or an annual report; it does not tell Acme Social Purpose Corporation whether the social purpose corporation form, the benefit corporation form, or an ordinary corporation is the right choice for its specific business or fundraising plans; it does not evaluate any specific special-purpose language for legal sufficiency; and it does not address the separate question of what happens to a pre-2015 "flexible purpose corporation" that has not amended its articles, beyond stating what the statute itself says about that scenario.

California's statute governing this entity form states its own name: "This division shall be known and may be cited as the Social Purpose Corporations Act." That name is not the one the Legislature originally used. The division was enacted in 2011 (Stats. 2011, Ch. 740) creating the "flexible purpose corporation," and the Legislature later renamed the form via SB 1301 (Stats. 2014, Ch. 694), effective January 1, 2015, substituting "social purpose corporation" throughout. The statute did not force existing entities to convert. A pre-2015 flexible purpose corporation may elect the new name by amending its articles — the statute states a corporation "may elect to change its status from a flexible purpose corporation to a social purpose corporation by amending its articles of incorporation to change its name to replace “flexible purpose corporation” with “social purpose corporation” and to replace the term “flexible purpose corporation” with “social purpose corporation” as applicable in any statements contained in the articles." — but a corporation that has not made that amendment keeps operating under the old name and the old statutory label: "For any flexible purpose corporation formed before January 1, 2015, that has not amended its articles of incorporation to change its status to a social purpose corporation, any reference in this division to social purpose corporation shall be deemed a reference to “flexible purpose corporation.”" The division's scope provision confirms the same continuity from the other direction, stating that the division applies to social purpose corporations "including all flexible purpose corporations formed under this division prior to January 1, 2015, and now existing"

citations.quote: This division shall be known and may be cited as the Social Purpose Corporations Act.

expectedJSON.gap: This is the current text of a division that has been amended repeatedly since 2011 (most recently by 2022 and 2023 chaptering shown in the fetched sections' own history notes); it does not track every intermediate version of the statute, only the version in force as of the checked date. It also does not identify whether any specific existing entity is, in fact, an unconverted flexible purpose corporation — that is a question about that entity's own articles of incorporation, not about the statute.

expectedJSON.body: A social purpose corporation is not governed only by Division 1.5. The statute makes California's general, Division 1 corporate law the default backdrop: "Except as otherwise expressly stated, the provisions of Division 1 (commencing with Section 100) shall apply to corporations organized under this division" In practice this means that matters this division does not address for a social purpose corporation — such as most shareholder meeting, voting, and inspection mechanics — are governed by the same General Corporation Law provisions that apply to an ordinary for-profit corporation, unless Division 1.5 itself states a different rule for social purpose corporations specifically.

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, incorporation by reference of the General Corporation Law (Division 1)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise expressly stated, the provisions of Division 1 (commencing with Section 100) shall apply to corporations organized under this division

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the general incorporation-by-reference rule only; it does not catalog every Division 1 section that applies, and it does not resolve a conflict between a specific Division 1.5 provision and a specific Division 1 provision for facts not addressed here — that requires reading both provisions together for the particular question at hand.

expectedJSON.body: A social purpose corporation is formed the same basic way as any other California corporation — by filing articles with the Secretary of State. The statute states: "One or more natural persons, partnerships, associations, social purpose corporations, or corporations, domestic or foreign, may form a social purpose corporation under this division by executing and filing articles of incorporation." and that "The corporate existence begins upon the filing of the articles and continues perpetually, unless otherwise expressly provided by law or in the articles." The articles must also flag the entity's form in its own name: the statute requires "The name of the social purpose corporation that shall contain the words “social purpose corporation” or an abbreviation of those words."

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, formation by filing articles of incorporation
citations.quote: One or more natural persons, partnerships, associations, social purpose corporations, or corporations, domestic or foreign, may form a social purpose corporation under this division by executing and filing articles of incorporation.

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, corporate existence begins on filing and continues perpetually absent a contrary provision
citations.quote: The corporate existence begins upon the filing of the articles and continues perpetually, unless otherwise expressly provided by law or in the articles.

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, required name element
citations.quote: The name of the social purpose corporation that shall contain the words “social purpose corporation” or an abbreviation of those words.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause covers only the act-of-filing and naming mechanics stated in this division; it does not restate the Secretary of State's separate name-distinguishability rules that apply to corporations generally under Division 1, and it does not address the filing fee, which the statute (Corp. Code § 2502.05) sets by cross-reference to the Government Code fee schedule for corporations generally rather than stating a dollar figure itself.

expectedJSON.body: What sets this entity form apart from an ordinary corporation is not the filing mechanics — it is what the articles must say about purpose. The statute requires a general-purpose statement drawn from a prescribed form; a corporation not organized to practice a licensed profession must state that "The purpose of this social purpose corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a social purpose corporation may be organized under Division 1.5 of the California Corporations Code" (with the corporation's own enumerated purposes filled in). Beyond that general statement, the articles must separately include "A statement that a purpose of the social purpose corporation, in addition to the purpose stated pursuant to paragraph (1), is to engage in one or more of the following enumerated purposes" one of the following two statutory categories: first, "One or more charitable or public purpose activities that a nonprofit public benefit corporation is authorized to carry out." or second, "The purpose of promoting positive effects of, or minimizing adverse effects of, the social purpose corporation’s activities upon any of the following, provided that the corporation consider the purpose in addition to or together with the financial interests of the shareholders and compliance with legal obligations, and take action consistent with that purpose:" — followed by a list of specific beneficiaries the statute itself supplies: the corporation's employees, suppliers, customers, and creditors; the community and society; or the environment. "Special purpose," as a defined statutory term, means exactly this articles-stated purpose: "“Special purpose” means the special purpose set forth in a social purpose corporation’s articles pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 2602."

citations.quote: The purpose of this social purpose corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a social purpose corporation may be organized under Division 1.5 of the California Corporations Code

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, required additional special-purpose statement and its lead-in language
citations.quote: A statement that a purpose of the social purpose corporation, in addition to the purpose stated pursuant to paragraph (1), is to engage in one or more of the following enumerated purposes

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, first enumerated special-purpose category (public-benefit-type activities)
citations.quote: One or more charitable or public purpose activities that a nonprofit public benefit corporation is authorized to carry out.

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, second enumerated special-purpose category (stakeholder and environmental effects)
citations.quote: The purpose of promoting positive effects of, or minimizing adverse effects of, the social purpose corporation’s activities upon any of the following, provided that the corporation consider the purpose in addition to or together with the financial interests of the shareholders and compliance with legal obligations, and take action consistent with that purpose:

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, statutory definition of "special purpose"
citations.quote: “Special purpose” means the special purpose set forth in a social purpose corporation’s articles pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 2602.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes the two statutory purpose categories and their required lead-in language; it does not draft the specific enumerated purpose to insert into either blank, does not address the separate prescribed purpose statement for a professional social purpose corporation (Corp. Code § 2602(b)(1)(B)) or for one subject to the Banking Law or Insurance Code (Corp. Code § 2602(b)(4)-(5)), and does not evaluate whether any specific proposed purpose text would satisfy the statute — that is a drafting judgment about the specific language chosen, not a fact this sheet can state in the abstract.

expectedJSON.body: Once formed, a social purpose corporation has broad business powers, but the statute makes those powers expressly conditional on the purpose the corporation put in its own articles: "Subject to any limitation contained in the articles, to compliance with any other applicable laws, and to consistency with the special purpose of the social purpose corporation, any social purpose corporation other than a social purpose corporation subject to the Banking Law or a professional social purpose corporation may engage in any business activity."

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, general business powers conditioned on consistency with the corporation's special purpose
citations.quote: Subject to any limitation contained in the articles, to compliance with any other applicable laws, and to consistency with the special purpose of the social purpose corporation, any social purpose corporation other than a social purpose corporation subject to the Banking Law or a professional social purpose corporation may engage in any business activity.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the general powers rule and its express purpose-consistency condition; it does not identify what counts as an activity inconsistent with a specific corporation's stated special purpose, which depends on the actual purpose language that corporation adopted, nor does it address the separate,  narrower powers rules that apply to a social purpose corporation subject to the Banking Law or organized as a professional corporation, which the same section (Corp. Code § 2604) addresses in its second sentence.

expectedJSON.body: This division sets its own director standard-of-care statute for a social purpose corporation, separate from the general corporate business-judgment-rule statute (Corp. Code § 309) that governs an ordinary corporation's directors. The core standard is worded the same way: "A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and with that care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances." But the factors a director is told to weigh are not the same. The statute states that "In discharging his or her duties, a director shall consider those factors, and give weight to those factors, as the director deems relevant, including the overall prospects of the social purpose corporation, the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and the purposes of the social purpose corporation as set forth in its articles." — expressly listing the articles-stated purposes of the social purpose corporation as one of the factors a director may consider and weigh, alongside the corporation's prospects and the shareholders' best interests, in a way the general corporate business-judgment-rule statute for an ordinary corporation does not.

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, director's core statutory duty of care
citations.quote: A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and with that care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, statutory factors a director may weigh, including the corporation's articles-stated purposes
citations.quote: In discharging his or her duties, a director shall consider those factors, and give weight to those factors, as the director deems relevant, including the overall prospects of the social purpose corporation, the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and the purposes of the social purpose corporation as set forth in its articles.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the statutory factors a director is permitted to consider; it does not state that a director is required to act on the special purpose in any particular instance — the statute's own wording gives the director discretion to decide how much weight each factor gets — and it does not address how a court would apply this standard to any specific board decision, since no California appellate authority construing this specific director-duty section was located in this research pass (see the CourtListener search note in this document's supporting research).

expectedJSON.body: Naming a stakeholder group or the environment in the articles' special-purpose statement does not give that group or the environment an enforceable stake in the corporation. The statute is direct about this: "Notwithstanding any of the purposes set forth in its articles, a social purpose corporation shall not be deemed to hold any of its assets for the benefit of any party other than its shareholders." — though the same subdivision preserves separately existing law by adding that "nothing in this division shall be construed as negating existing charitable trust principles or the Attorney General’s authority to enforce any charitable trust created." The following subdivision closes the loop for directors specifically: "Nothing in this section, express or implied, is intended to create or grant or shall create or grant any right in or for any person or any cause of action by or for any person, and a director shall not be responsible to any party other than the social purpose corporation and its shareholders."

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, statement that the corporation does not hold assets for the benefit of any party other than its shareholders
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any of the purposes set forth in its articles, a social purpose corporation shall not be deemed to hold any of its assets for the benefit of any party other than its shareholders.

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, preservation of existing charitable trust law and Attorney General enforcement authority
citations.quote: nothing in this division shall be construed as negating existing charitable trust principles or the Attorney General’s authority to enforce any charitable trust created.

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, no third-party right or cause of action created; director responsible only to the corporation and its shareholders
citations.quote: Nothing in this section, express or implied, is intended to create or grant or shall create or grant any right in or for any person or any cause of action by or for any person, and a director shall not be responsible to any party other than the social purpose corporation and its shareholders.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states what the statute itself says about who may enforce a social purpose corporation's special purpose and who its assets are held for; it does not address whether a different body of law outside this division — such as a specific charitable trust already in existence, or a separate contractual promise the corporation made to a named stakeholder — could independently create an enforceable right, since the statute expressly carves out that possibility without itself resolving whether one exists in any given case.

expectedJSON.body: A social purpose corporation's board has a recurring, statute-driven reporting duty to its own shareholders. The statute states a deadline: "The board of a social purpose corporation shall cause an annual report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 120 days after the close of the fiscal year." Beyond ordinary financial statements, the same section requires a distinct narrative document: "The board shall cause to be provided with the annual report, a management discussion and analysis (special purpose MD&A) concerning the social purpose corporation’s stated purpose or purposes as set forth in its articles pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 2602, and, to the extent consistent with reasonable confidentiality requirements, shall cause the special purpose MD&A to be made publicly available by posting it on the social purpose corporation’s Internet Web site or providing it through similar electronic means."

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, 120-day deadline for the annual report to shareholders
citations.quote: The board of a social purpose corporation shall cause an annual report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 120 days after the close of the fiscal year.

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, required special purpose management discussion and analysis (special purpose MD&A)
citations.quote: The board shall cause to be provided with the annual report, a management discussion and analysis (special purpose MD&A) concerning the social purpose corporation’s stated purpose or purposes as set forth in its articles pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 2602, and, to the extent consistent with reasonable confidentiality requirements, shall cause the special purpose MD&A to be made publicly available by posting it on the social purpose corporation’s Internet Web site or providing it through similar electronic means.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause covers the annual report and special purpose MD&A requirement running to shareholders under this division; it does not address the separate, narrower exception for a corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record (covered in this document's small-corporation clause) or the separate compliance path available to a corporation already reporting under the federal Securities Exchange Act (Corp. Code § 3502(h)), and it is not a claim that this reporting duty is the same as, or satisfies, the different annual benefit report this corpus's Benefit Corporation document describes for the separate benefit-corporation statute.

expectedJSON.body: Beyond the annual report, this division imposes an interim reporting duty that does not have a counterpart in this corpus's existing Benefit Corporation document. The statute requires: "The board shall cause a special purpose current report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 45 days following the occurrence of any one or more of the events specified in subdivision (b) or (c)" Among the triggering events the same section lists is a board or management decision to "Determine that the special purpose has been satisfied or should no longer be pursued, whether temporarily or permanently."

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, 45-day deadline for a special purpose current report following a triggering event
citations.quote: The board shall cause a special purpose current report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 45 days following the occurrence of any one or more of the events specified in subdivision (b) or (c)

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, one statutory triggering event for a special purpose current report
citations.quote: Determine that the special purpose has been satisfied or should no longer be pursued, whether temporarily or permanently.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states only the reporting deadline and one of several statutory triggering events; it does not list every triggering event the same section defines (material expenditures and withheld planned expenditures are also covered, in Corp. Code § 3501(b) and (c)(1), and are not quoted here), and it does not address the good-faith forward-looking-statement liability exclusion the statute separately provides for these reports (Corp. Code § 3502(d)).

expectedJSON.body: The statute relaxes the accounting standard for the financial statements required in the annual and current reports for a small social purpose corporation: "The financial statements of any social purpose corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record of its shares, determined as provided in Section 605, required to be furnished by Sections 3500 and 3501 are not required to be prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles if they reasonably set forth the assets and liabilities and the income and expense of the social purpose corporation and disclose the accounting basis used in their preparation."

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, relaxed financial-statement standard for a corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record
citations.quote: The financial statements of any social purpose corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record of its shares, determined as provided in Section 605, required to be furnished by Sections 3500 and 3501 are not required to be prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles if they reasonably set forth the assets and liabilities and the income and expense of the social purpose corporation and disclose the accounting basis used in their preparation.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the numeric shareholder-count threshold and the alternative disclosure standard the statute substitutes for GAAP; it does not address how "holders of record," cross-referenced to Corp. Code § 605, is counted in any specific ownership structure (for example, shares held in street name or through a nominee), which depends on the facts of that structure.

expectedJSON.body: The statute attaches personal liability to a false statutory report. It states that "Any officers, directors, employees, or agents of a social purpose corporation who do any of the following shall be liable jointly and severally for all the damages resulting therefrom to the social purpose corporation or any person injured by those actions who relied on those actions or to both:" — and one of the listed acts triggering that liability is to "Make, issue, deliver, or publish any prospectus, report, including the reports required pursuant to Sections 3500 and 3501, circular, certificate, financial statement, balance sheet, public notice, or document respecting the social purpose corporation or its shares, assets, liabilities, capital, dividends, business, earnings, or accounts which is false in any material respect, knowing it to be false, or participate in the making, issuance, delivery, or publication thereof with knowledge that the same is false in a material respect."

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, introductory joint-and-several liability standard for a false statutory report
citations.quote: Any officers, directors, employees, or agents of a social purpose corporation who do any of the following shall be liable jointly and severally for all the damages resulting therefrom to the social purpose corporation or any person injured by those actions who relied on those actions or to both:

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, liability for knowingly publishing a false report respecting the corporation
citations.quote: Make, issue, deliver, or publish any prospectus, report, including the reports required pursuant to Sections 3500 and 3501, circular, certificate, financial statement, balance sheet, public notice, or document respecting the social purpose corporation or its shares, assets, liabilities, capital, dividends, business, earnings, or accounts which is false in any material respect, knowing it to be false, or participate in the making, issuance, delivery, or publication thereof with knowledge that the same is false in a material respect.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes the introductory liability standard and one of the four listed acts that trigger it (Corp. Code § 3503(a)); the other three listed acts — false book or record entries, altering records with intent to deceive, and a knowing material omission from a required report — are not separately quoted here. This clause does not address how a court would apply the knowledge and materiality requirements to any specific report's contents.
